nodes.name: Grading type
nodes.statement: A grading type is an abelian group beta together with group homomorphisms \[ shift : Z to beta, sign : beta to \pm 1\, \] such that sign(shift(1)) = -1; that is, the differential, which has degree shift(1), is odd. For a degree d in beta we write (-1)^d := sign(d) for its Koszul sign.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.GradingType}

A grading type is an abelian group $\beta$ together with group homomorphisms
\[
  \operatorname{shift} : \mathbb{Z} \to \beta,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{sign} : \beta \to \{\pm 1\},
\]
such that $\operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{shift}(1)) = -1$; that is, the
differential, which has degree $\operatorname{shift}(1)$, is odd. For a degree
$d \in \beta$ we write $(-1)^d := \operatorname{sign}(d)$ for its Koszul sign.
nodes.clean_text: A grading type is an abelian group beta together with group homomorphisms \[ shift : Z to beta, sign : beta to \pm 1\, \] such that sign(shift(1)) = -1; that is, the differential, which has degree shift(1), is odd. For a degree d in beta we write (-1)^d := sign(d) for its Koszul sign.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType

nodes.statement: shift : Z to beta, sign : beta to \pm 1\,
nodes.raw_latex:
\[
  \operatorname{shift} : \mathbb{Z} \to \beta,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{sign} : \beta \to \{\pm 1\},
\]
nodes.clean_text: shift : Z to beta, sign : beta to \pm 1\,

nodes.name: Sign of an integer shift
nodes.statement: For every integer n one has (-1)^shift(n) = (-1)^n.
conclusions: For every integer n one has (-1)^shift(n) = (-1)^n.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.sign_shift}


For every integer $n$ one has $(-1)^{\operatorname{shift}(n)} = (-1)^n$.
nodes.clean_text: For every integer n one has (-1)^shift(n) = (-1)^n.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.sign_shift

nodes.statement: Since shift(n) = n cdot shift(1) and sign is a homomorphism, (-1)^shift(n) = sign(shift(1))^n = (-1)^n.
nodes.raw_latex:
Since $\operatorname{shift}(n) = n \cdot \operatorname{shift}(1)$ and
$\operatorname{sign}$ is a homomorphism,
$(-1)^{\operatorname{shift}(n)} = \operatorname{sign}(\operatorname{shift}(1))^n = (-1)^n$.
nodes.clean_text: Since shift(n) = n cdot shift(1) and sign is a homomorphism, (-1)^shift(n) = sign(shift(1))^n = (-1)^n.

nodes.name: Standard gradings
nodes.statement: The integers Z form a grading type with shift the identity and sign(n) = (-1)^n. The parities Z/2 form a grading type with shift the reduction modulo 2 and sign(p) = (-1)^p.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.GradingType.standard}


The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ form a grading type with $\operatorname{shift}$ the
identity and $\operatorname{sign}(n) = (-1)^n$. The parities $\mathbb{Z}/2$
form a grading type with $\operatorname{shift}$ the reduction modulo $2$ and
$\operatorname{sign}(p) = (-1)^p$.
nodes.clean_text: The integers Z form a grading type with shift the identity and sign(n) = (-1)^n. The parities Z/2 form a grading type with shift the reduction modulo 2 and sign(p) = (-1)^p.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType.standard

nodes.name: Product gradings
nodes.statement: Let beta be a grading type and gamma an abelian group. The product beta times gamma is a grading type with shift(n) = (shift(n), 0) in two ways: either the sign is read off the first factor alone, sign(b,c) = (-1)^b, or, when gamma is a grading type as well, the sign is the total sign sign(b,c) = (-1)^b\,(-1)^c. Neither choice is canonical, so both are constructions to be activated locally rather than instances.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.GradingType.prod}


Let $\beta$ be a grading type and $\gamma$ an abelian group. The product
$\beta \times \gamma$ is a grading type with
$\operatorname{shift}(n) = (\operatorname{shift}(n), 0)$ in two ways: either
the sign is read off the first factor alone, $\operatorname{sign}(b,c) = (-1)^b$,
or, when $\gamma$ is a grading type as well, the sign is the total sign
$\operatorname{sign}(b,c) = (-1)^b\,(-1)^c$. Neither choice is canonical, so
both are constructions to be activated locally rather than instances.

Neither choice is canonical, so both are constructions to be activated locally rather than instances.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradingType.prod

nodes.name: Graded linear map
nodes.statement: Let R be a semiring and let M, N be beta-indexed families of R-modules. A graded R-linear map f : M to N of degree d in beta consists of an R-linear map f_i,j : M(i) to N(j) for every pair of degrees with i + d = j. Graded linear maps of degree d form an R-module under componentwise operations.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearMap}

Let $R$ be a semiring and let $M, N$ be $\beta$-indexed families of $R$-modules.
A graded $R$-linear map $f : M \to N$ of degree $d \in \beta$ consists of an
$R$-linear map $f_{i,j} : M(i) \to N(j)$ for every pair of degrees with
$i + d = j$. Graded linear maps of degree $d$ form an $R$-module under
componentwise operations.

Graded linear maps of degree d form an R-module under componentwise operations.
nodes.label: AInfinityTheory.GradedLinearMap

nodes.name: Composition of graded linear maps
nodes.statement: The composite of graded linear maps of degrees d and e is a graded linear map of degree d + e, whose component from degree i factors through degree i + d. The identity is a graded linear map of degree 0. Composition is associative and unital.
conclusions: The composite of graded linear maps of degrees d and e is a graded linear map of degree d + e, whose component from degree i factors through degree i + d.
The identity is a graded linear map of degree 0.

nodes.name: Graded multilinear map
nodes.statement: Let R be a semiring, let (M_j)_j in iota be a finite family of beta-indexed families of R-modules, and let N be a beta-indexed family of R-modules. A graded R-multilinear map of degree d in beta consists, for every choice of input degrees (d_j)_j in iota and every output degree i with sum_j d_j + d = i, of an R-multilinear map \[ prod_j M_j(d_j) to N(i). \] Graded multilinear maps of degree d form an R-module under componentwise operations.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{AInfinityTheory.GradedMultilinearMap}

Let $R$ be a semiring, let $(M_j)_{j \in \iota}$ be a finite family of
$\beta$-indexed families of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be a $\beta$-indexed family of
$R$-modules. A graded $R$-multilinear map of degree $d \in \beta$ consists, for every
choice of input degrees $(d_j)_{j \in \iota}$ and every output degree $i$ with
$\sum_j d_j + d = i$, of an $R$-multilinear map
\[
  \prod_j M_j(d_j) \to N(i).
\]
Graded multilinear maps of degree $d$ form an $R$-module under componentwise
operations.

nodes.name: \Ainf{}-composition
nodes.statement: An Ainf-composition on a graded quiver Hom assigns to every positive arity n and every string of objects X_0,dots,X_n a graded multilinear map \[ m_n : Hom(X_0,X_1) times cdots times Hom(X_n-1,X_n) to Hom(X_0,X_n) \] of degree shift(2-n). nodes.name: Stasheff sign
nodes.statement: The sign pm 1 attached to (r,s,t) is \[ prod_k=r+s^n-1 (-1)^\|a_k\|, \|a_k\| := |a_k| - shift(1), \] the product of the Koszul signs of the reduced degrees of the t trailing inputs. Since the sign character is a homomorphism, this equals (-1)^|a_r+s| + cdots + |a_n-1| - shift(t).

\label{AInfinityTheory.stasheffSign}

  \|a_k\| := |a_k| - \operatorname{shift}(1),
\]
the product of the Koszul signs of the reduced degrees of the $t$ trailing
inputs. Since the sign character is a homomorphism, this equals
$(-1)^{|a_{r+s}| + \cdots + |a_{n-1}| - \operatorname{shift}(t)}$.

nodes.raw_latex:
Fix a commutative ring $R$. The $\KLRW$ category of $1$ black strand
  and $n$ red strands, denoted $\KLRW$ category of $1$ black strand
  and $n$ red strands, denoted $\KLRW^R_n$, is given by
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $\Ob(\KLRW^R_n)$ is the set of positionings of $1$ black strand
    with $n$ red strands
    \item $\Hom(X, Y)$ is the free $R$-module generated by $\StrandSpace_{X, Y}$.
  \end{itemize}
  Composition in $\KLRW^R_n$ is defined by extending the composition of elements of the strand
  space linearly.

  Since each $\Hom(X, Y)$ is an $R$-module and composition is $R$-linear, $\KLRW^R_n$
  is $R$-linear and thus preadditive.
